title: Family & people
goal: Talk about your family, say who people are, and use 'my, your, his' and the possessive -को.
intro:
Family is at the centre of Nepali life, and the vocabulary is rich: there are different words for older and younger brothers and sisters, and for uncles on your father's and mother's side. These words are also used to address strangers — you'll call people दाइ, दिदी, भाइ and बहिनी every day.

Grammar in this unit: the possessive **-को** (and its forms -का, -की), possessive pronouns like मेरो 'my', the plural ending **-हरू**, and how to say 'I have a brother'.

grammar.title: Possession: -को, -का, -की and 'my, your…'
grammar.body:
'Of' is **-को** attached to the owner, and the owner comes first: राम**को** घर 'Ram's house', नेपाल**को** राजधानी 'the capital of Nepal'.

-को behaves like an adjective ending in -ओ and can agree with the thing owned:
**-को** before a singular noun · **-का** before a plural or respected noun · **-की** before a female noun.
In everyday Kathmandu speech -को is used almost everywhere, but -की is kept with women (मेरी आमा, उसकी दिदी) and -का with respected men (मेरा बुबा).

Pronoun possessives:
म → **मेरो** · हामी → **हाम्रो** · तँ → **तेरो** · तिमी → **तिम्रो** · तपाईं → **तपाईंको**
ऊ → **उसको** · उनी → **उनको** · उहाँ → **उहाँको** · उनीहरू → **उनीहरूको** · यो → **यसको** · त्यो → **त्यसको** · को 'who' → **कसको** 'whose'.

examples.en: My older sister is a doctor.

grammar.title: Gender and plural
grammar.body:
Nepali nouns have **no grammatical gender** for things: a table or a house is neither masculine nor feminine. Gender matters only for **people and animals** that are female, and mostly in careful speech (मेरी बहिनी, उनी गइन् 'she went').

The plural ending is **-हरू** *-haru*: केटा → केटाहरू 'boys', साथी → साथीहरू 'friends'. It is often left out when the plural is obvious, especially after a number (दुई जना साथी 'two friends'). Adding -हरू to a name or relative means 'X and co.': आमाहरू 'mum and the others'.

Respect works like plural: a respected person (बुबा, उहाँ, तपाईं) takes **plural-looking** agreement — मेरा बुबा, not मेरो बुबा.

examples.en: Where are didi and the others?

grammar.title: Saying 'I have…' for family
grammar.body:
Nepali has no verb 'to have'. For relatives (and body parts) use **possessive + छ**: 'my brother is' = 'I have a brother'. The verb agrees with the relative: a respected older relative takes हुनुहुन्छ.

मेरो एउटा भाइ **छ**। 'I have a younger brother.'
मेरा दुई जना दाइ **हुनुहुन्छ**। 'I have two older brothers.'
मेरो दिदी **छैन**। 'I don't have an older sister.'

(For things you carry or own, Nepali uses **सँग** 'with' instead — मसँग पैसा छ 'I have money' — which you'll meet in unit 12.)

examples.en: I don't have an older sister.

dialogue.setting: Sita shows Sarah a photo of her family on her phone.

lines.en: That's my son, the youngest. He's four.

culture: Nepalis rarely use each other's first names with elders or older siblings — you say **दाइ**, **दिदी**, **काका**, **आमा** instead, and you can attach them to a name (राम दाइ, सीता दिदी). Birth order is so important that it shows up in nicknames: the eldest son is often **जेठा**, the second **माइला**, the third **साइला**, the youngest **कान्छा** (girls: जेठी, माइली, साइली, कान्छी). Many families still live as joint families with grandparents, and newly married women traditionally move into the husband's home. In-laws and elders are addressed with **हजुर** and the respectful verb forms.

tip.title: 'My', 'your', 'Ram's': -को
tip.body:
- 'Of' is **-को** stuck to the owner, and the owner comes first: राम**को** घर 'Ram's house'.
- म → **मेरो**, हामी → **हाम्रो**, तिमी → **तिम्रो**, तपाईं → **तपाईंको**.
- It can agree: **-की** before a woman (मेरी आमा), **-का** before a respected man or a plural (मेरा बुबा).

tip.title: 'I have a brother'
tip.body:
- There's no verb 'to have'. For relatives say 'my brother **is**': मेरो एउटा भाइ **छ**.
- The verb agrees with the relative: plural **छन्**, a respected elder **हुनुहुन्छ**.
- 'I don't have…' uses **छैन** / **छैनन्**: मेरो दाइ **छैन**.

tip.title: Women, men and more than one
tip.body:
- Things have no gender, but **women** do: मेरी श्रीमती, तिम्री बहिनी (-ई); a respected man takes **-आ**: मेरा श्रीमान्.
- Plural is **-हरू**: केटा → केटा**हरू** 'boys'. Skip it after a number: दुई जना छोरा 'two sons'.
- Plural and respected people take plural verbs: छन्, छैनन्.
tip.pattern: मेरी + woman  ·  मेरा + respected man  ·  noun + हरू

new: मेरो एउटा छोरा र एउटी छोरी छन्।

sentences.en: Is that girl your little sister?
How many children do you have?

tip.title: An uncle for every side
tip.body:
- Nepali has a word for each relative: **काका** (dad's younger brother) and **काकी**; **मामा** (mum's brother — not 'mum'!) and **माइजु**; **फुपू** (dad's sister).
- Elders get respect: **मेरा** काका, verb **हुनुहुन्छ**.
- Call them by the kin word, not their name: काका, चिया खानुहुन्छ?

sentences.native: मेरा हजुरबुबा र हजुरआमा पाटनमा बस्नुहुन्छ।
sentences.roman: merā hajurbubā ra hajurāmā Pāṭanmā basnuhunchha.

sentences.en: My uncle (mum's brother) is in India.
Auntie, would you like some tea?
Who's in your family? (to a friend)
There are four of us in our family.

sentences.native: मेरो परिवारमा आमा, बुबा र एउटा भाइ छन्।
sentences.roman: mero pariwārmā āmā, bubā ra euṭā bhāi chhan.
sentences.en: In my family there's mum, dad and a younger brother.
